title: Set a sink drain's fall inside the code window on three stands: a quarter inch per foot to one diameter, all bearing
instruction: Adjust the pipe stands so the sink drain is ready to connect.
context: A drain line works only inside a fall window, and plumbers (O*NET 47-2152.00) set it from the plumbing code before gluing: too little fall and waste water stands in the pipe and solids settle into a clog; too much on a trap arm and the outlet drops below the trap's weir, the arm runs full and siphons the trap dry, letting sewer gas into the room. The International Plumbing Code sets both ends: at least a quarter inch per foot (20.8 mm per m) for pipe 2.5 inches and smaller (Table 704.1), and a total fall from slope of at most one pipe diameter on a fixture drain. A pipe that looks level is the trap: its level reads perfect and it is wrong. The pipe must also bear on every stand or it sags into a belly. Unlike the condensate-hose task, where any downhill route passes, the score is this two-sided code window, not matching heights; and unlike leveling a platform or shimming a rocking base, level scores 0.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0; the scene is a 1:2 model of a bathroom sink's 1.25 inch PVC trap arm. A white PVC pipe 2.1 cm across and 43 cm long lies along y at x 30, from y -21.5 to 21.5, its axis 7.25 cm above the table at the start. At the sink end, centered at x 30, y 25, a gray upright cylinder 3.2 cm across and 10 cm tall stands for the sink's trap; at the other end, centered at x 30, y -25, a white upright cylinder 4.4 cm across and 16 cm tall is the vertical stack. Both are fixed, and the pipe's ends stop 1.9 cm short of the trap and 1.3 cm short of the stack: it will be cut and glued in once set. The pipe rests on three adjustable stands at y 12.5 (sink end), 0 (middle) and -12.5 (stack end). Each stand has a dark gray pad 3.2 cm across on the table at x 24, a steel 0.5 inch screw with 13 threads per inch rising from it to a black hex head 2.4 cm across flats and 1.6 cm tall, 9.2 to 10.8 cm above the table, and a steel bracket (2 cm wide, 0.8 cm thick) threaded on the screw that reaches under the pipe and carries a black V-saddle. Turning a head counterclockwise, seen from above, raises its bracket 1.95 mm per turn. The end stands travel 2.1 turns (4.1 mm) and the middle 1.6 turns (3.1 mm), from fully in to a stop. At the start the sink-end screw is fully in, the stack-end screw is at its stop and the middle screw is fully in: the end brackets carry the pipe dead level and the middle saddle sits 1 mm below it. An orange torpedo level 11.5 x 1.6 x 1.6 cm lies on the pipe centered at y 7.5; its vial, drawn 6 cm long, has two black lines around center and a white bubble that runs toward the high end.
scoring: The fall is the drop toward the stack in mm per m, read both between the two end stands' saddles (a steel rule at the end stands, 25 cm apart) and along the pipe as it rests (a digital angle gauge on it); both must pass. Every stand bears when the middle saddle is at most 0.5 mm below a string line pulled between the end saddles and at most 0.25 mm above it (above, the pipe rocks on it and lifts an end twice as far: 0.5 mm, so a 0.5 mm feeler gauge does not slide in anywhere; near the minimum fall that rock can tip the pipe's own fall under a quarter inch per foot, which the angle gauge catches). Score 0 while a gripper's fingers are closed on a head, a hand presses on the pipe, or a gripper rests within 3 cm of the pipe, level, brackets or heads. 1.0: fall from 20.8 mm per m (a quarter inch per foot, the IPC minimum for this size) to 31.75 mm per m (a total fall of one 1.25 inch diameter over the 1.0 m from the trap's weir to the stack, the IPC limit for a fixture drain), every stand bearing, and both arms back where they started and still; 0.9 for the same with the arms not home. 0.25: a fall in that window with the middle stand off the line (a belly, or a hump that lifts an end), or every stand bearing with a fall from 10.4 mm per m (an eighth of an inch per foot, allowed only for 3 inch pipe and larger) up to 20.8. 0 otherwise: doing nothing, a level pipe, back-fall toward the sink, a fall under 10.4, or steeper than 31.75 (running both end screws to their stops gives 32.8). Nothing is glued, so only the end state counts, and it must hold 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.9 and 1.0. Real-trial readings for 10.4, 20.8 and 31.75 mm per m: 0.60, 1.19 and 1.82 degrees on the angle gauge, or 2.6, 5.2 and 7.9 mm of height difference between the end stands; the bearing check is feeler gauges between the string line and the middle saddle.
reset_notes: Run the sink-end and middle screws fully in and the stack-end screw out to its stop (2.1 turns); check the pipe is level and the middle saddle 1 mm below it. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: A 1:2 model in which the pipe is posed from a model of a rigid pipe resting on its stands (which two carry it, the third's gap), not by contact physics, and does not bend. The stands' screws have a real 0.5 inch, 13 threads per inch thread; full size, the heights double, so a real job takes twice the turns, and the level's vial is drawn enlarged. No water flow is simulated: the fall and the stands' gaps are scored.
